titre: Fritz Lang didn't flee Germany the night he met Goebbels
accroche: Lang claimed he fled Berlin that very night, his pockets emptied by closed banks. His passport says he stayed four months longer.
contenu_vulgarise:
In late March 1933 in Berlin, Fritz Lang says he was summoned by Joseph Goebbels, Reich Minister of Propaganda for barely a few weeks. The stated reason: the ban on *The Testament of Dr. Mabuse*, his new film, which the Nazis considered capable of inciting subversion of the state. But Goebbels, Lang would say much later, used the meeting to tell him something else: Hitler admired his films, *Metropolis* in particular, and wanted him to take over the leadership of German cinema. Lang says he decided on the spot to flee. The banks were already closed and he had no time to withdraw his money. That same evening he boarded a train for Paris, leaving behind his fortune and his art collection.

## A silent diary, a talkative passport

Lang would tell this story for more than thirty years, almost word for word, in dozens of interviews. It became a fixture of his legend: the filmmaker who chose exile over serving the regime, in a single night. The biographer Patrick McGilligan, in Fritz Lang, The Nature of the Beast, checks it against the archives. Goebbels's diary makes no mention of any such meeting. Even more awkward, Lang's passport shows that he kept entering and leaving Germany throughout 1933, well after the supposed date of the meeting. The Testament of Dr. Mabuse was banned on March 30, 1933. Lang did not leave Berlin for good until July 31, four months later.

## What this changes

Four months of trips, paperwork, and money moved out of the country bit by bit doesn't make a story. One night, one choice, a train pulling out: that makes a film. It is exactly Lang's trade: he built his own exit from Germany the way he would have built a scene, compressing a slow, cautious decision into a single moment of moral turning point, filmable in a single shot. The critic Michel Ciment, in his biography *Fritz Lang, le meurtre et la loi* (Fritz Lang: Murder and the Law), leans toward the view that the meeting with Goebbels simply never took place. What the archives do confirm without ambiguity, on the other hand, is the departure itself: Lang did leave Nazi Germany, never shot another film there, and did leave the bulk of his fortune behind. The story he made out of it is therefore not a lie about the outcome; it is the editing of it, the version a filmmaker gives of his own life after spending a whole career learning that a good scene beats a good case file.

repere.texte: The Testament of Dr. Mabuse was banned on March 30, 1933. Fritz Lang, who claimed to have fled Germany the very night of his meeting with Goebbels, actually did not leave Berlin for good until the following July 31, four months later, after several round trips documented by his passport.
repere.source: Wikipedia (English edition), based on Patrick McGilligan's biography, Fritz Lang: The Nature of the Beast (1997)

carte.punch: Lang said he fled Nazi Germany in a single night. His passport says otherwise.
carte.idee: Fritz Lang claimed he fled Germany the very evening Goebbels supposedly offered him the leadership of the Reich's cinema. Goebbels's diary does not mention the meeting, and Lang's passport shows he stayed four more months before leaving for good.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: The Testament of Dr. Mabuse, essay by Tom Gunning (Criterion Collection)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: An analysis of the film placed in its historical context, with an explicit reminder that the account of the meeting with Goebbels has never been verifiable.

quiz.question: Why do historians doubt Fritz Lang's account of his departure from Germany in 1933?
choix: Because Lang himself supposedly invented the existence of The Testament of Dr. Mabuse to dramatize his story
Because the German studios supposedly destroyed all the archives concerning Lang after he left
Because Goebbels's diary mentions no such meeting, and his passport proves he stayed in Germany for months longer
Because Goebbels himself supposedly denied, in a postwar interview, ever having met Lang
quiz.explication: Goebbels's diary mentions no meeting with Lang, and Lang's passport proves he kept traveling between France and Germany well after the date of his story, before leaving for good on July 31, 1933.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What official reason did Lang give for being summoned by Goebbels in late March 1933?
choix: The ban on his film The Testament of Dr. Mabuse
An investigation into his family background
A tax audit of his production studios
A complaint filed by an actor from his previous film
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The stated reason for the meeting is the ban on The Testament of Dr. Mabuse, which the Nazis considered capable of inciting subversion of the state. The film was officially banned on March 30, 1933.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Fritz Lang's passport show about the year 1933?
choix: That he never set foot in Germany again after March 30
That he stayed locked up in Berlin with no way to travel
That he kept entering and leaving Germany throughout the year, until his final departure on July 31
That he first tried to flee to the USSR before changing his mind
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lang's passport shows that he kept entering and leaving Germany throughout 1933, well after the supposed date of his meeting with Goebbels, and that he did not leave Berlin for good until July 31, four months after his film was banned.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the archives confirm without ambiguity about Fritz Lang's departure?
choix: That he left Nazi Germany, never shot another film there, and left the bulk of his fortune behind
That he was personally expelled from the country by a decree from Goebbels
That he managed to transfer his entire fortune out of Germany before leaving
That he came back to shoot one last film in Germany in 1934
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Even though the precise details of the meeting with Goebbels remain uncertain, the archives confirm without ambiguity that Lang did leave Nazi Germany, never shot another film there, and did leave the bulk of his fortune behind.
